title: Government Sells Coal India Stake at a 10 Percent Discount. The Stock Drops 4 Percent in Minutes.
excerpt: India is selling up to 2 percent of Coal India through an offer for sale at ₹412 per share — ₹46 below the previous close. The ₹5,000 crore sale is part of an ₹80,000 crore disinvestment target that is already behind schedule. NRI investors are watching.
body:
India's government launched the sale of up to 2 percent of Coal India on Wednesday morning, pricing the offer for sale at ₹412 per share — a 10 percent discount to the stock's previous closing price of ₹458. The stock responded immediately, dropping more than 4 percent in early trade to ₹437.45 as the market absorbed the dilution.

## The Deal

The base offer involves 1 percent of Coal India's equity, with a green shoe option to sell an additional 1 percent if demand warrants it. At the ₹412 floor price, the government expects to raise approximately ₹5,000 crore (about $520 million).

Non-retail investors — mutual funds, insurance companies, foreign portfolio investors — can bid on May 27 and 28. Retail investors, including eligible Coal India employees, get their window on May 29. The staggered structure is designed to allow institutional price discovery before retail participation.

Coal India is India's largest coal producer and the world's largest by output volume. The government currently holds 63.13 percent of the company. Even after the full 2 percent sale, it will retain a commanding majority.

## Why Now

The timing is driven by fiscal arithmetic. India has set a disinvestment target of ₹80,000 crore for fiscal year 2027 (April 2026 to March 2027), part of a broader asset monetisation strategy to fund infrastructure spending without expanding the fiscal deficit.

With the fiscal year nearly two months old and the target largely untouched, the Coal India OFS is among the first major moves. But ₹5,000 crore against an ₹80,000 crore target is a modest start, and the discount pricing suggests the government is prioritising certainty of execution over price maximisation.

The Iran war has complicated the calculus. Oil at $98 a barrel is straining government finances through higher fuel subsidies, and the rupee at 95.60 against the dollar is increasing the cost of dollar-denominated imports. Disinvestment proceeds help plug the gap without additional borrowing.

## Coal India's Fundamentals

Despite the stock's immediate reaction to the OFS, Coal India's operational performance has been strong. The company reported robust Q4 FY2026 results, with production volumes holding steady and dividend payouts remaining attractive. At ₹412, the stock offers a dividend yield that exceeds most bank fixed deposit rates — a factor the government is counting on to attract retail investors on May 29.

Coal India's business is also structurally insulated from some of the risks that are rattling other sectors. India's electricity demand hit an all-time record of 270.82 gigawatts earlier this week during the heatwave, and coal-fired power plants supplied the bulk of that load. Twenty-one plants were running on critical coal stocks. Demand for coal is not declining — it is at an all-time high.

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRI investors, Coal India has long been a proxy for India's energy demand story — a high-dividend, state-backed blue chip with limited downside risk. The OFS creates a rare opportunity to buy at a government-mandated discount, but the logistics of participating from abroad are not straightforward.

Non-resident Indians with active demat accounts and NRE/NRO bank accounts can participate in the retail window on May 29. However, the OFS mechanism requires same-day settlement through the stock exchange, and not all NRI-friendly brokerages support OFS participation. HDFC Securities, ICICI Direct, and Zerodha are among those that do, but NRIs should verify eligibility and settlement timelines before bidding.

The broader question for diaspora investors is whether Coal India remains a sound long-term holding in a world that is ostensibly moving toward clean energy. India's answer, at least for the current decade, is unambiguous: coal generates approximately 55 percent of the country's electricity, demand is rising faster than renewable capacity can be built, and Coal India is the irreplaceable supplier. The energy transition is real, but in India, it is a 20-year story, not a 5-year one.

## What Comes Next

The ₹80,000 crore disinvestment target will require several more rounds of sales — potentially in ONGC, NHPC, BPCL, and other public sector enterprises. The Coal India OFS is a test case: if it generates strong demand at ₹412, the government will have proof of concept for a busy disinvestment calendar. If it struggles, expect a rethink on pricing strategy and timing.

For the market, the immediate impact is a short-term overhang on Coal India's stock. The 4 percent drop reflects dilution anxiety, not fundamental deterioration. Once the OFS is absorbed — likely by Thursday evening — the stock should stabilise near its pre-OFS range, unless broader market conditions (oil, Iran, rupee) deteriorate further.

The lesson for NRI investors: government stake sales in India's blue-chip PSUs are among the few structural buying opportunities that come with a built-in discount. The trick is being positioned to act when they happen.
